## 1. Learning objectives
After this lesson you can:
- explain **generics**: the `<String>` in `ArrayList<String>` tells the compiler what the list holds, so mistakes are found when you compile, not when a customer is waiting;
- pick the right collection: **List** (ordered, repeats allowed), **Set** (no repeats), **Map** (find a value by its key);
- write a generic class (`Counter<T>`) and a generic method (`<T extends Comparable<T>> T largest(...)`);
- sort with a **Comparator** (`Comparator.comparing(...)`, `.reversed()`, `.thenComparing(...)`);
- move the app's product list into a `Map` and explain why lookup becomes a single step.

## 2. Plain-English explanation
- **The problem generics solve.** Since lesson 07 you have written `ArrayList<Product>`. The part in `< >` is a **type parameter**. Without it a list could hold anything, and you would have to guess what comes out. With it, `products.add("banana")` simply does not compile. A *generic class* is a class written once with a placeholder (`T`) that each user fills in: `Counter<String>` counts names, `Counter<PaymentMethod>` counts payment methods.
- **A generic method** puts its own placeholder before the return type: `static <T> List<T> distinct(List<T> items)`. `T extends Comparable<T>` means "any type that knows how to compare itself", so the method may call `compareTo`.
- **Three families of collection.**
  | Collection | Order | Repeats | Find by | In this lesson |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | `List` (`ArrayList`) | the order you add | allowed | position (`get(2)`) | the sales log |
  | `Set` (`HashSet`, `TreeSet`) | none (`TreeSet`: sorted) | **never** | "is it in there?" (`contains`) | `buyerNames()` |
  | `Map` (`HashMap`, `LinkedHashMap`, `TreeMap`) | none (`LinkedHashMap`: as added; `TreeMap`: sorted) | keys never repeat | the **key** (`get("rice")`) | the products |
- **Why the app uses a Map now.** Until lesson 16 `Inventory.findProduct` looked at every product one by one. With 4 products nobody notices; with 4,000 it is slow. A `Map<String, Product>` jumps straight to the answer. The key is the cleaned, lower-case name (`"rice 25kg"`), so `"  RICE   25kg "` still finds the same product. We use a `LinkedHashMap` so the products still come out in the order they were added, and the stock report does not change.
- **Comparator.** To sort numbers or strings Java already knows the order. For *your* objects you say which value to compare: `Comparator.comparingInt(Product::getQuantity)` means "fewest units first". `.reversed()` flips it; `.thenComparing(...)` breaks ties, so the order is always the same (important for tests).
- **Intentional refactor in this lesson.** `Inventory` swaps its `ArrayList<Product>` for a `Map`. Only the *inside* changes. Every public method keeps its name and behaviour, so **every earlier test stays green without any edit** (only the version line checked by `MainTest` changes). That is the proof the refactor is safe (lesson 24 comes back to this idea).
- **A copy keeps the data safe.** `products()` and `sortedProducts(...)` return **copies**. Sorting a copy never reorders the real list.
- **New in the app:** `Counter<T>` (count anything), `ProductOrder` (ready-made comparators), and in `Inventory`: `sortedProducts(order)`, `unitsSoldByProduct()`, `bestSellers(n)` and `buyerNames()`.

```

Map<String, Integer> stock = new LinkedHashMap<>();
stock.put("rice", 12);
stock.merge("rice", 8, Integer::sum); // rice was 12, now 20
```

## 7. Common mistakes and troubleshooting
| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `incompatible types: String cannot be converted to Product` | Wrong type put into a generic collection | That is generics working: pass a `Product`, or change the list's type |
| `unexpected type; required: reference, found: int` for `List<int>` | Type parameters must be objects | Use the wrapper: `List<Integer>`, `Map<String, Integer>` |
| `map.get("rice")` is `null` | The key is missing (the Map's answer for "not there") | Use `getOrDefault("rice", 0)` or check `containsKey` |
| A product is "not found" although it exists | Stored under one spelling, looked up under another | Always build the key with the same `key(name)` method |
| `UnsupportedOperationException` on `products().add(...)` | `List.copyOf` and `List.of` make read-only lists | Add through `Inventory.addProduct`; copy to `new ArrayList<>(...)` if you need a changeable list |
| A `HashSet` prints in a surprising order | A `HashSet` has no order | Use `LinkedHashSet` (as added) or `TreeSet` (sorted) |
| `ConcurrentModificationException` | The list was changed while a `for` loop walked it | Collect the changes first, apply them after the loop |
| A custom class is "not found" in a `Set` or as a `Map` key | It has no `equals` / `hashCode` (records get both for free) | Make it a record, or write both methods |
